# Decoding and Structured Output {#sec-decoding}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** The measurements were run on the same Turkish
product-review corpus as @sec-bake-off and @sec-classification, on a balanced
sample so that accuracy reads against a 50% floor. Two models were used
deliberately — `qwen3.5:9b` and `llama3.2:3b` — because
@sec-decoding-constrained's finding is that constrained decoding buys almost
nothing on one and a great deal on the other. Software: `ollama` 0.24.0,
Python 3.14.5. The sampling explorer below is fully functional. Two things about the runs that the
rest of this chapter depends on and that are worth pinning wherever you repeat
them: the model tags resolve to `ollama`'s default 4-bit quantisation, which
changes the logit distribution and is therefore part of every calibration
number in @sec-decoding-logprobs; and each latency figure below is a single
timed run on a laptop, so read the ratios rather than the seconds and treat
anything under about 1.5× as within the noise of a warm machine.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- explain what each sampling parameter does to the probability distribution;
- make a model emit schema-valid output whenever it is allowed to finish;
- use logprobs for confidence, routing, and abstention;
- diagnose repetition and degeneration instead of tuning parameters at random.

## Greedy, beam, temperature, top-k / top-p / min-p {#sec-decoding-sampling}

A language model's forward pass ends in a vector of **logits** — one raw
score per vocabulary token. Everything in @sec-transformers was about
producing that vector. What happens next is not learning; it is a
[sampling policy you control at inference time]{.hl}, and it changes the
character of the output more than most people expect.

- **Temperature** $\tau$ rescales logits before the softmax:
  $p_i \propto \exp(z_i/\tau)$. Low $\tau$ sharpens, high $\tau$ flattens.
- **Top-k** keeps only the $k$ highest-probability tokens, then renormalises.
- **Top-p (nucleus)** keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative
  probability reaches $p$, then renormalises [@holtzman2020curious].

**The order these run in matters, and it is the part that surprises people.**
In `transformers`, one decoding step applies the
repetition/frequency/presence penalties to the raw logits, then temperature,
then top-k, then top-p, then min-p, and then samples. vLLM also applies the
penalties and then temperature first, but runs min-p *before* top-k and top-p;
llama.cpp's default chain applies temperature *last*, after all the cutoffs.
So the order is fixed inside one library, not across libraries — check the one
you use. Two consequences follow for the temperature-first order.
Because temperature runs *before* top-p, raising the temperature changes which
tokens fall inside the nucleus — so the common claim that temperature "only
changes the contrast, never the ranking" is true of temperature alone and
misleading in a pipeline that also truncates; the explorer below lets you watch
the nucleus change membership. And because the penalties run *before*
temperature (in all three libraries), the same penalty value bites far harder
at $\tau = 0.2$ than at $\tau = 1.5$: an additive penalty $\alpha$ on the raw
logit becomes $\alpha/\tau$ after scaling. If you are tuning both, tune the
temperature first.

at the current temperature, before any cutoff; teal bars show what survives
your sampling policy, after renormalisation. Try $\tau = 0.2$, then
$\tau = 1.8$. Then cut the tail with top-p $= 0.6$.

```{=html}
<div class="widget-title">Sampling policy explorer — the same logits, reshaped</div>
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof temperature = Inputs.range([0.1, 2.0], { value: 1.0, step: 0.05, label: "Temperature τ" })
```
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof topK = Inputs.range([1, 12], { value: 12, step: 1, label: "Top-k" })
```
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof topP = Inputs.range([0.05, 1.0], { value: 1.0, step: 0.05, label: "Top-p (nucleus)" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
samplingDist = {
  const candidates = [
    { token: "exhausted",   logit:  4.2 },
    { token: "confused",    logit:  3.7 },
    { token: "silent",      logit:  3.1 },
    { token: "inspired",    logit:  2.9 },
    { token: "lost",        logit:  2.5 },
    { token: "quiet",       logit:  2.2 },
    { token: "bored",       logit:  1.8 },
    { token: "energized",   logit:  1.4 },
    { token: "hungry",      logit:  1.0 },
    { token: "transformed", logit:  0.5 },
    { token: "purple",      logit: -0.5 },
    { token: "recursive",   logit: -1.2 }
  ];

  // 1) temperature-scaled softmax
  const ws = candidates.map(d => Math.exp(d.logit / temperature));
  const Z = ws.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  let rows = candidates
    .map((d, i) => ({ ...d, p: ws[i] / Z }))
    .sort((a, b) => b.p - a.p);

  // 2) top-k filter
  rows = rows.map((d, i) => ({ ...d, kept: i < topK }));

  // 3) top-p (nucleus) filter over what survived top-k,
  //    measured on the top-k survivors renormalised to sum to 1
  const massK = rows.filter(d => d.kept).reduce((a, d) => a + d.p, 0);
  let cum = 0;
  rows = rows.map(d => {
    const before = cum;
    if (d.kept) cum += d.p / massK;
    return { ...d, kept: d.kept && before < topP };
  });

  // 4) renormalize the survivors
  const Zk = rows.filter(d => d.kept).reduce((a, d) => a + d.p, 0) || 1;
  return rows.map(d => ({ ...d, pFinal: d.kept ? d.p / Zk : 0 }));
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: 640,
  height: 380,
  marginLeft: 100,
  x: {
    label: "P(next token)",
    domain: [0, Math.max(0.4, ...samplingDist.map(d => d.pFinal), ...samplingDist.map(d => d.p)) * 1.15],
    tickFormat: ".0%"
  },
  y: { domain: samplingDist.map(d => d.token), label: null },
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(samplingDist, { y: "token", x: "p", fill: "#D4DADF" }),
    Plot.barX(samplingDist.filter(d => d.kept), { y: "token", x: "pFinal", fill: "#0E7C7B" }),
    Plot.text(samplingDist.filter(d => d.kept), {
      y: "token", x: "pFinal",
      text: d => (d.pFinal * 100).toFixed(1) + "%",
      dx: 6, textAnchor: "start", fill: "#5B6272", fontSize: 11
    }),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`**${samplingDist.filter(d => d.kept).length} of 12** candidate tokens survive
this policy. Gray = softmax at τ = ${temperature.toFixed(2)}, before any cutoff; teal =
renormalised sampling distribution.`
```
:::

Notice what a low temperature does *not* do: it never changes the ranking,
only the contrast. Top-k and top-p, by comparison, are hard cutoffs — they
exist mainly to stop the model from ever picking `recursive` in a sentence
about tired students. This trio is the cheapest lever you have in every
applied system from here on.

### Greedy, beam, and min-p

Three more policies complete the picture.

**Greedy** takes the argmax at every step. It is temperature 0 in the limit,
and it is the right default whenever there is one correct answer. (APIs treat
"temperature 0" as a request for greedy decoding, since dividing by zero is
undefined. Even then a hosted API may not return the same string every time:
batching and floating-point rounding on the GPU can change a near-tie between
two tokens, and after one different token the rest of the text differs too.)

**Beam search** keeps the *k* best partial sequences (*k* is the *beam
width*) and extends all of them, so it searches for a high-probability *whole
sequence* rather than choosing the best token at each step. It is still a
search with a limited width, so it can miss the single most probable sequence.

@sec-machine-translation measures it properly on translation, and two of its
findings are worth carrying here. The gains die quickly — beam 1 to 2 bought
+0.61 BLEU, and beam 2 to 64 bought +0.57 more for seven times the compute.
And the widely repeated warning that wider beams make the output *worse* (the
"curse of beam search") did not appear at all, most likely because the decoder
normalised by length during the search. Length normalisation divides a beam's
log-probability by its length; without it, every extra token adds another
negative log-probability, so the search prefers outputs that are too short.

**Min-p** [@nguyen2024minp] is the newer cutoff. Where top-p keeps a fixed
*mass* and top-k a fixed *count*, min-p keeps every token whose probability is
at least a fraction of the top token's:

$$
\text{keep } i \quad\text{if}\quad p_i \;\ge\; m \cdot \max_j p_j
$$

That makes the cutoff adapt to the shape of the distribution rather than to a
constant. Typical values of $m$ are 0.05–0.1: with $m = 0.1$ and a top token
at 0.6, every token below 0.06 is cut.

When the model is confident — one token at 0.9 — min-p keeps almost nothing,
which is what you want. When it is genuinely uncertain across twenty plausible
continuations, min-p keeps them all, where top-p 0.9 would cut the last few by
cumulative mass alone, however plausible they are.

::: {.column-margin}
The general rule underneath all five: [the policy should depend on how many
good answers the task has]{.hl}. Extraction, classification and translation
have one, so greedy or a narrow beam. Drafting, brainstorming and dialogue
have many, so sample. @sec-machine-translation measured the cost of getting
this backwards — a chat-default temperature of 1.0 took a translation model
from 30.17 BLEU to 14.34.
:::

**What we will look at.** First why greedy decoding walks into repetition
loops, and why the usual penalties are the wrong tool once you are generating
structure. Then constrained decoding, where a grammar makes invalid output
unreachable rather than unlikely — measured on two models, because it buys
almost nothing on one and seventeen accuracy points on the other. Then tool
calls, the case where the strong-model result does not let you off. Then
logprobs, which discriminate well, calibrate badly, and still buy you accuracy
for the price of one threshold. And finally streaming, which wants the
opposite of everything structured output wants.

## Repetition and degeneration {#sec-decoding-repetition}

Greedy and low-temperature decoding have a characteristic failure: the model
falls into a loop and repeats a phrase until it hits the token limit.

The mechanism is not mysterious. Having produced a phrase once, the model has
made that phrase part of its own context, and a language model trained on real
text has learned that repeated phrases are more likely after the first
repetition.

@holtzman2020curious named this and showed the surprising part: the loop is
not a low-probability accident. **The repeated continuation is often the
single highest-probability sequence available**, which is why greedy decoding
walks into it and sampling rarely does.

The usual controls, and what each costs:

| control | what it does | what it breaks |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Sampling (top-p, min-p) | takes a non-argmax token sometimes, breaking the loop | variety you may not want in an extraction task |
| Repetition penalty | lowers the logit of any already-used token — dividing it when positive, multiplying when negative (see below) | punishes legitimately repeated words — names, technical terms, `null` |
| No-repeat n-gram | forbids any n-gram already emitted | forbids real repeated phrases; ruinous in structured output where `{"type":` recurs |
| Presence penalty | a flat subtraction the first time a token appears | same failure mode, milder; does not escalate |
| Frequency penalty | a subtraction proportional to how often it has appeared | escalates with every repeat, so long outputs drift |

: Five ways to stop a loop, and what each one costs {tbl-colwidths="[26,38,36]"}

The repetition penalty $\theta$ acts on the raw logit, and its sign handling is
the part implementations get wrong:

$$
z_i' = \begin{cases} z_i / \theta & z_i \ge 0 \\ z_i \cdot \theta & z_i < 0 \end{cases}
$$

Dividing a *negative* logit by $\theta > 1$ raises it towards zero — that is a
reward, not a penalty — which is why the two branches are not cosmetic. The
penalty comes from CTRL [@keskar2019ctrl], whose formula simply divides; the
sign case was added by later implementations such as `transformers`. The
OpenAI-style penalties avoid the problem by being additive and acting on counts
instead:
$z_i' = z_i - \alpha_{\text{presence}}\,\mathbb{1}[c_i > 0] - \alpha_{\text{freq}}\,c_i$,
where $c_i$ is how many times token $i$ has already appeared. Presence fires
once; frequency keeps scaling.

[The penalties are blunt instruments and they are the wrong tool for
structured output.]{.hl} A JSON object legitimately repeats keys, braces and
quote characters; a no-repeat-3-gram constraint on JSON is a way to guarantee
invalid output. If you are generating structure, the fix for repetition is the
grammar in @sec-decoding-constrained, not a penalty.

## Constrained decoding {#sec-decoding-constrained}

Everything above reshapes a distribution over the whole vocabulary.
[Constrained decoding](#gloss-constrained-decoding){#term-constrained-decoding .term-ref}
does something stricter: at each step it computes which tokens could legally
continue the output under a grammar, and sets the logits of all the others to
$-\infty$. Invalid output stops being unlikely and becomes **unreachable** —
with three conditions on that word. The schema has to be one the library
actually supports, since unsupported keywords are commonly ignored rather than
enforced. The generation has to *finish*: a run that hits your token limit, a
timeout, or a dropped connection leaves a prefix that is legal so far and
invalid as a document. And a grammar constrains structure, not semantics, so a
required field can be filled with a plausible fabrication. Parse and validate
the result anyway; the guarantee is worth a lot and it is not "never check".

::: {#gloss-constrained-decoding .column-margin .term-gloss}
**constrained decoding** — masking the logits at each step to the tokens a
grammar allows. Guarantees the *shape* of a completed generation and says
nothing about whether it is true. [↩](#term-constrained-decoding){.term-back}
:::

One property of that mechanism is easy to miss and worth stating before the
measurements, because it bounds what they mean. **Masking at each step is not
the same as sampling from the model's distribution conditioned on the
grammar.** A token that is locally legal may lead only to dead ends, and local
masking has no way to renormalise for that — so what you get is a distribution
over grammatical strings whose likelihoods are no longer proportional to the
model's own [@park2024grammar]. In practice it shows up as grammatical output
the unconstrained model would have ranked lower. Grammar-aligned decoding fixes
it at extra cost; every library in @sec-decoding-tools ships the cheap,
distorting version, which is the right default and worth knowing you are using.

::: {.fig-cap}
The machinery is a finite-state machine over the tokenizer's vocabulary
[@willard2023efficient]: compile the regex — or a JSON Schema whose nesting is
bounded — into an automaton, track which state you are in, and precompute for
each state the set of allowed next tokens. A general context-free grammar does
*not* fit in a finite-state machine, because unbounded nesting needs a stack;
libraries that accept a CFG run an incremental parser (a pushdown automaton)
instead, which costs more per step and buys back arbitrary recursion. @geng2023grammar is the same idea for general
structured NLP tasks.
:::
::::

### What it actually buys

The interesting question is not whether a grammar can enforce a schema — it
can — but **where an unenforced model stops complying on its own**, and what
enforcement costs when it takes over. Four schemas of increasing awkwardness,
150 balanced reviews, two models, asked-versus-enforced:

```text
qwen3.5:9b                        parses  schema-ok  accuracy  s/item
  L1 flat, natural enum   asked   100.0%      98.0%     89.3%    1.23
  L1 flat, natural enum   forced  100.0%     100.0%     88.7%    1.30
  L2 unnatural enum       asked    99.3%      99.3%     86.7%    1.33
  L2 unnatural enum       forced  100.0%     100.0%     87.3%    1.36
  L3 nested + array       asked   100.0%      98.7%     88.0%    1.44
  L3 nested + array       forced  100.0%     100.0%     88.0%    1.62
  L4 nested + nullable    asked   100.0%      98.0%     88.7%    1.73
  L4 nested + nullable    forced  100.0%     100.0%     88.7%    1.74

llama3.2:3b                       parses  schema-ok  accuracy  s/item
  L1 flat, natural enum   asked    98.0%      98.0%     83.3%    0.37
  L1 flat, natural enum   forced  100.0%     100.0%     85.3%    0.56
  L2 unnatural enum       asked    99.3%      97.3%     78.0%    0.43
  L2 unnatural enum       forced  100.0%     100.0%     80.0%    5.13
  L3 nested + array       asked    79.3%      79.3%     70.7%    0.37
  L3 nested + array       forced  100.0%     100.0%     88.0%    0.70
  L4 nested + nullable    asked    99.3%      98.7%     86.0%    0.53
  L4 nested + nullable    forced  100.0%     100.0%     86.7%    9.26
```

Three findings, and the first is the one that reframes the technique.

**On a strong model, the grammar buys almost nothing.** `qwen3.5:9b` complied
with the schema 98–99.3% of the time when merely *asked*, at every difficulty
level including nested objects with a nullable field. Enforcement took that to
100% and left accuracy unchanged. [Modern instruction-tuned models mostly
produce the JSON you describe; the grammar is insurance on the last one or two
percent.]{.hl}

**Two qualifications on that null result (no difference found), and they
matter more than the result itself.**
First, it is a null on 150 items: the 95% interval around an 88% accuracy is
roughly ±5 points, so this experiment could not have detected a two- to
five-point degradation even if one were there. Second, the task here is
*classification*. @tam2024format found that format restriction **helps**
classification and **hurts** multi-step reasoning — GSM8K-style tasks lost
several points under JSON mode with near-zero parsing failures, which locates
the loss in the reasoning rather than in the parsing. So this chapter's result
is a narrow subset of theirs rather than a contradiction of it, and it does not
license the general claim. Do not carry "enforcement is free" into a
chain-of-thought task; the safe pattern there is to let the model reason
unconstrained and constrain only the final answer field.

**On a weak model, it is the difference between working and not.**
`llama3.2:3b` fell to **79.3% schema-valid** on the nested-plus-array schema —
one output in five unusable. Enforcement took it to 100%, and **accuracy rose
from 70.7% to 88.0%**, a 17.3-point gain, because the malformed fifth had been
scored as wrong. The grammar did not make the model smarter; it stopped a
formatting failure from being counted as a reasoning failure.

**The cost is latency, and it is not where you would guess.** Overhead ranged
from **1.01× to 17.5×**; the top of that range is the weak model at L4, where
0.53 s per item became 9.26 s. The overhead was not monotone in schema complexity — L1 and L3 were cheap, L2 and L4 expensive.
The two ends sit on different models, which is itself the finding: on
`qwen3.5:9b` the grammar costs between 1.006× and 1.13× — **essentially
free** — and on `llama3.2:3b` between 1.5× and 17.5×. A grammar is cheap where
the model already agrees with the schema and expensive where it does not.

The two expensive ones share a property: the schema demands something the
model does not want to produce, an unnatural enum in one case and a nullable
field in the other. That is consistent with the grammar having to fight the
model's distribution rather than ride it, though this measurement establishes
the pattern rather than the mechanism.

::: {.column-margin}
Which is a reason to measure rather than reason about it. If the grammar's
cost depended only on schema complexity you could budget for it from the
schema; it appears to depend on the *disagreement* between the schema and the
model, which you cannot see without running both.
:::

### What it cannot fix

A grammar constrains shape. It has no access to truth, and the failure this
produces is worth seeing directly. From @sec-sequence-labeling-llm, where a
schema demanded an object with an integer `answer`:

```text
POST /api/generate   format={"answer": integer}
prompt: "What is the capital of France?"
  ->  {"answer": 1}
```

Schema-valid, parseable, type-correct, and meaningless. [Constrained decoding
converts a parse failure into a semantic failure]{.hl}, which is usually the
trade you want — a wrong value you can validate beats a crash — but it is a
trade, not a fix. Every guarantee it gives you is syntactic.

Two corollaries worth stating plainly:

1. **Validate values, not just structure.** An enum is checkable; a free-text
   field is not. Push as much of your contract into enumerable types as the
   task allows.
2. **A schema is not a substitute for the escape hatch.** If the model has no
   legal way to say *I do not know*, the grammar guarantees it will say
   something else instead. Add `null` to the type, and — as
   @sec-sequence-labeling found — check that the model actually uses it.

## Making tool arguments reliable {#sec-decoding-tool-args}

The highest-leverage use of everything above is not extraction; it is tool
calls. A tool call *is* a structured output — a function name and a typed
argument object — and it has a property that makes correctness matter more
than usual: **something executes afterwards.**

A malformed summary is a bad summary. A malformed argument object is either a
crash or, worse, a call that succeeds with the wrong value.

How this looks in practice: with *function calling*, you send the model a list
of tool definitions, each a name, a description and a JSON Schema for its
arguments, and the model replies with a tool name and an argument object
instead of prose. Whether those arguments are *enforced* depends on a flag.
Hosted APIs usually offer two strengths. A "JSON mode" guarantees only that the
output is syntactically valid JSON, not that it matches your schema; a
schema-enforced mode (OpenAI's API, for example, calls it `strict`) compiles
your schema into the kind of grammar described above. Know which one you have
switched on.

Three rules follow from the measurements above.

**Constrain the arguments, always.** This is the case where the strong-model
result does not let you off. 98% schema-validity is excellent for extraction
and unacceptable for execution: at a thousand calls a day it is twenty
failures a day, each one a stack trace or a wrong action. The grammar takes
that to zero for every call that finishes. Its latency cost is real and varies
by schema, but you can measure it before you ship.

**Type the arguments as narrowly as the tool allows.** An enum of four
operations cannot be called with a fifth. A date typed as a string can be
`"yesterday"`; typed with a pattern, it cannot. Every constraint you can push
into the schema is a validation you do not have to write and an error class
that becomes unreachable.

**A valid call is still not a correct call.** The grammar guarantees
`{"operation": "delete", "id": 4}` is well-formed. It does not know whether 4
was the right id, and @sec-tool-design is where that problem — and the
confirmation and authorisation machinery around it — belongs.

## Logprobs, confidence, and abstention {#sec-decoding-logprobs}

Alongside each token, the model reports the log probability it assigned — its
[logprob](#gloss-logprob){#term-logprob .term-ref}. This is the cheapest
signal available about how sure the model is, it costs nothing extra to
obtain, and most pipelines throw it away.

The question is whether it is *usable*. Measured with `qwen3.5:9b` on 400
balanced reviews, with
the answer constrained to a single token — `A` for positive, `B` for negative
— so that the first generated token *is* the answer and its probability can be
renormalised over just those two alternatives into a proper binary
probability.

::: {#gloss-logprob .column-margin .term-gloss}
**logprob** — the log probability the model assigned to a token. Interpretable
as confidence only when the answer is a single token; for a long answer, the
mean logprob mostly measures how ordinary the phrasing was.
[↩](#term-logprob){.term-back}
:::

### It discriminates

The first question about any confidence signal is whether it orders items
correctly — whether the ones it is sure about really are the ones it gets
right. Two AUCs answer that:

```text
accuracy                                              86.75%
AUC of P(positive) against the true label             0.9492
AUC of confidence for predicting its own correctness  0.8268

mean confidence when the model was right              0.9481
mean confidence when the model was wrong              0.7793
```

[The score is good and the model knows when it is guessing.]{.hl} An AUC of
0.9492 says the probability ranks positives above negatives almost as well as
a trained classifier would; 0.8268 says confidence separates the model's own
correct answers from its incorrect ones. @kadavath2022language is the general
version of that second result.

### It is not calibrated

Discrimination and calibration are different properties, and the second one
fails. The table groups the 400 answers by stated confidence; ECE (expected
calibration error, defined in @sec-classification) is the gap between
confidence and accuracy in each bin, averaged with the bin sizes as weights:

```text
confidence bin      n    accuracy   mean confidence
[0.50, 0.55)       15       33.3%             52.4%
[0.55, 0.60)       10       50.0%             57.5%
[0.60, 0.65)       10       70.0%             62.5%
[0.65, 0.70)        8       62.5%             66.4%
[0.70, 0.75)        7       85.7%             72.7%
[0.75, 0.80)        8       87.5%             77.6%
[0.80, 0.85)       13       61.5%             82.7%
[0.85, 0.90)       20       85.0%             87.6%
[0.90, 0.95)       25       68.0%             92.6%
[0.95, 1.00)      284       95.1%             99.4%

ECE = 7.04%
```

The table uses ten equal-width bins over $[0.50, 1.00)$. Always say which
bins you used, because ECE is sensitive to that choice, and this binning is
not flattering anyone: 284 of the 400 items
land in the top bin, which alone contributes about 44% of the 7.04%. An
equal-mass binning, or a Brier score — which needs no bins at all — is the more
honest summary of the same data.

Two things to read here, and they are not equally solid. The model is
**overconfident in the middle**: the bin it called 92.6% likely was right 17 of
25 times, a 68.0% rate whose 95% Wilson interval runs $[48, 83]$ — entirely
below the confidence it stated. That is the firm finding.

The one people quote is the bottom bin, and it deserves more caution than it
usually gets: 5 correct out of 15, a 33.3% point estimate with an interval of
$[15, 58]$. That interval contains 50%, so this does not establish "below
chance" — and a wide interval is not evidence of uselessness either. What this
bin does establish is narrower: **a label probability near 0.5 is not a
calibrated estimate of being right**, on fifteen items. (The model reports a
log-probability; 0.5 is the probability, which is about $-0.69$ in logs. Convert
before you threshold.)

[Do not read a label probability near 0.5 as "right half the time".]{.hl} What
it may still be good for is *ordering*: an uncalibrated score can rank documents
well enough to route the doubtful ones to a human, which is exactly what the
abstention experiment below does. Judge that use on an accuracy–coverage curve,
not on this bin.

Two fixes, in order of effort. **Temperature scaling** [@guo2017calibration]
fits a single scalar $T$ on a held-out slice and divides the logits by it — the
same $\exp(z/\tau)$ from @sec-decoding-sampling, used after the fact instead of
during generation. Because it is monotone it leaves the AUC and the abstention
curve of the next section *exactly* unchanged while typically cutting ECE by a
factor of two or more, so there is no reason not to try it first. What one
scalar can fix is a *systematic* overconfidence, like the top bins here; it
cannot remove the bin-to-bin zigzag in the middle of the table. If one scalar
is not enough, @sec-classification's isotonic or Platt map is the next step.

### It is immediately useful for abstention

Even uncalibrated, the ranking is enough to route:

```text
abstain on the least-confident    kept    accuracy on what is kept
                            0%     400                     86.75%
                            5%     380                     89.47%
                           10%     360                     90.83%
                           20%     320                     92.50%
                           30%     280                     95.00%
                           50%     200                     97.50%
```

**Sending the least-confident fifth to a human, or to a larger model, takes
accuracy on the retained items from 86.75% to 92.50%** without changing the
model at all. Read the denominator: 92.50% is the model's accuracy on the 320
it kept, not the accuracy of the whole pipeline. What the other 80 cost — a
human's error rate, or a bigger model's — is not measured here, and the
end-to-end number is the coverage-weighted combination of the two. Report
accuracy *and* coverage together, always. Even so it is a larger gain than most
prompt engineering produces, and it costs one threshold.

::: {.column-margin}
This is the cheapest routing signal in the book, and it composes with
everything else: abstain below a threshold, escalate the abstained items to a
bigger model, and report coverage alongside accuracy. Note that the
threshold is a *fitted quantity* and belongs on a held-out slice — the same
discipline @sec-classification applied to its decision threshold. Choosing it
on the data you report is the same mistake in new clothes.
:::

Those last two tables describe the same 400 reviews. Side by side, they show
why a broken calibration does not stop you from using the signal:

### The caveat that limits all of it

This worked because the answer was **one token from a two-token alphabet**.
That is the easiest possible case, and the technique degrades quickly away
from it:

- **Multi-token answers.** The mean logprob over a sentence mostly measures
  how *ordinary the phrasing* was, not how likely the content is to be true.
- **Open-ended generation.** There is no "the answer token" to read.
- **Long structured output.** The probability of a well-formed JSON object is
  dominated by its punctuation, which the model is certain about.

Which is a design argument as much as a caveat: **if you want a confidence
signal, structure the task so the answer is one constrained token.** Such
labels need not cost accuracy: in @sec-prompting's comparison of twelve prompt
variants, the one with the meaningless labels `A`/`B` finished second, more
than ten points ahead of `olumlu`/`olumsuz`.

## Streaming and incremental parsing {#sec-decoding-streaming}

Streaming exists because users react to the latency they *perceive*, not the
one you measure. A response that takes four seconds to arrive complete feels
slower than the same response whose first words appear in two hundred
milliseconds — even when both finish at the same moment, so no throughput
metric can tell them apart.

The tension with everything above is that **structured output and streaming
want opposite things**. A JSON object is only parseable once its last brace
arrives, so the natural implementation buffers the whole response and streams
nothing. Three ways out, in increasing order of effort:

| approach | what the user sees | cost |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Buffer and validate | nothing, then everything | simplest; the full latency is perceived |
| Incremental parse | fields appear as they complete | a parser that accepts prefixes; partial states are visible |
| Split the call | prose streams, structure arrives after | two calls, and they can disagree with each other |

: Streaming against structure {tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

The middle row is the one worth building, and the thing to get right is that
**a partial parse is a different type from a complete one**. `{"duygu": "olu`
is not a bad object; it is an incomplete one, and a consumer that cannot
represent *not yet known* will either crash or render garbage. Model it
explicitly — a field is missing, pending, or present — rather than letting
`None` mean two things.

One practical note follows from @sec-decoding-constrained: a grammar and an
incremental parser are the same automaton looked at from two ends.

If you are already constraining generation, the state machine that decides
which tokens are legal is also the one that can tell a consumer which fields
are final. Most stacks do not connect the two, and it is a reasonable thing to
build when the interface warrants it.

## Intuition checks {#sec-decoding-intuition}

Answer each one before you open it. The first follows from the algebra; the
other five are questions this chapter settled with a measurement rather than
an argument.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Does lowering temperature make the model more accurate?

It makes it more *deterministic*, which is not the same thing. Temperature
rescales the logits before the softmax, so it changes the contrast between
options and never the ranking — the argmax token at $\tau = 0.1$ is the argmax
token at $\tau = 1.9$.

So if greedy decoding gets an item wrong, lowering the temperature will not
fix it; it will only make the model wrong more reliably. What temperature
controls is variance. Lowering it *can* raise the accuracy of sampled output —
each draw lands on the argmax more often, which is what @sec-machine-translation
saw at temperature 1.0 — but only up to greedy's accuracy, never beyond it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Your JSON parse failure rate is 2%. Is constrained decoding worth it?

It depends entirely on what happens next. For extraction into a table, 2% is a
retry and a shrug. For **tool calls, 2% is a wrong action or a stack trace on
every fiftieth request**, and the answer is yes without further discussion.

Then measure the cost rather than assuming it is small: overhead here ranged
from 1.01× to 17.5×, worst where the schema demanded something the model did not
want to produce.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. A grammar guarantees valid JSON. What does it not guarantee?

Anything about the content. Measured in @sec-sequence-labeling-llm: a schema demanding
an integer `answer` returned `{"answer": 1}` for the capital of France —
valid, typed, parseable, meaningless.

Constrained decoding converts parse failures into semantic failures. That is
usually the trade you want, because a wrong value can be validated and a crash
cannot, but it is a trade. Push what you can into enums, validate values
separately from structure, and give the model a legal way to say *I do not
know*.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Your weak model is 79% schema-valid. Is it a bad model?

Partly, but less than the number suggests. Measured here: `llama3.2:3b` at
79.3% schema-validity on a nested schema scored **70.7% accuracy** — and with
the grammar turned on, 100% valid and **88.0% accurate**.

Seventeen of those points were never a reasoning failure; they were a
formatting failure being counted as one. Before concluding a small model
cannot do your task, make sure you are measuring the task rather than its
punctuation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. The model says it is 92% confident. Should you believe it?

Not as a probability. Measured on 400 items: the bin of answers the model
rated 0.90–0.95 was right **68.0%** of the time. Expected calibration error
was 7.04%, and the bin nearest probability 0.5 was right **33.3%** on 15 items — an interval
wide enough to contain chance, and too wide to prove anything except that the
number is not a calibrated probability.

But the *ranking* was good — AUC 0.8268 for predicting its own correctness —
which is enough to route on. Use logprobs to order items, not to quote
percentages, and calibrate on a held-out slice if you need the number itself.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. You want a confidence score for a free-text answer. How?

Not by averaging the logprobs, which mostly measures how ordinary the phrasing
was rather than how likely the content is to be right.

Restructure the task instead. Ask for the answer *and* a single constrained
token that classifies it — a verdict, a category, a yes/no — and read the
logprob of that token. This chapter's abstention curve works because the
answer was one token from a two-token alphabet; that property is something you
design in, not something you find.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-decoding-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** These recur in the two
credible open sources this book uses, plus the ones this chapter's own
measurements make answerable.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the mechanism

**Q: What does temperature actually do?**

Rescales the logits before the softmax, $p_i \propto \exp(z_i/\tau)$. Say the
consequence that shows you have thought about it: **it never changes the
ranking**, only the contrast, so temperature cannot fix a wrong argmax. Then
distinguish it from top-k and top-p, which are hard cutoffs that remove
candidates entirely, and from min-p, whose cutoff scales with the top token's
probability so it adapts to how peaked the distribution is.

**Q: How does constrained decoding work?**

Compile the schema into an automaton over the tokenizer's vocabulary, and at
each step mask the logits of every token that could not legally continue.
Invalid output becomes unreachable rather than unlikely. The good follow-up:
it guarantees syntax and nothing else, and it costs latency — measured here
from 1.01× to 17.5×, worst when the schema demands something the model does not
want to produce.

**Q: Why is beam search standard in translation and absent from chat?**

Because beam search looks for the highest-probability *sequence*, which is
what you want when the task has approximately one right answer and actively
not what you want when it has many: in open-ended text the most probable
sequence tends to be bland and repetitive [@holtzman2020curious].
@sec-machine-translation measured the cost of confusing the two in the other
direction, sampling where one answer was wanted: a chat-default temperature of 1.0 took a translation
model from 30.17 BLEU to 14.34.

### Testing whether you have shipped one

**Q: Tool calls fail in production about 2% of the time. What do you do?**

Constrain the arguments — this is the case where 98% is not good enough,
because something executes afterwards. Then narrow the types: enums for
operations, patterns for dates, so whole error classes become unreachable.
Then verify the constraint is actually applied, because a server that ignores
`format` fails silently. And say clearly that a valid call is still not a
correct call: the id may be well-typed and wrong, which is
@sec-tool-design's problem rather than the decoder's.

**Q: How would you make your system say "I don't know"?**

Give it a legal way to — a `null` in the schema or an explicit abstain value —
and then a threshold to decide when to use it. Constrain the answer to a
single token, read its logprob, and pick a threshold on a held-out slice.
Measured here: abstaining on the least-confident 20% took accuracy from 86.75%
to 92.50%, no model change involved. Report coverage alongside accuracy, or
the number is meaningless.

**Q: Your evaluation says the model is 92% confident and it is right 68% of
the time. What is wrong?**

Nothing is wrong; you are reading a discrimination signal as a calibration
one. The logprob ranked answers well — AUC 0.8268 for predicting its own
correctness — while being badly calibrated, at 7.04% ECE. Use the ordering to
route and calibrate on held-out data if you need the number itself.
@sec-classification has the machinery.

| Python | 3.14.5 | `json.loads` from the stdlib parses; the twenty lines around it are our own checks for required fields and enum values, since parsing is not schema validation. The abstention curve uses `numpy`, which is not stdlib |

: The stack these numbers came from {tbl-colwidths="[24,16,60]"}

Worth knowing about, not used above:

| library | current version | when you would reach for it |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `outlines` | 1.3.3 | the reference implementation of the automaton in @sec-decoding-constrained [@willard2023efficient]; use it when you need the grammar in your own process rather than behind a server flag |
| `xgrammar` | 0.2.5 | the same idea optimised for throughput; what to reach for when the 17.5× overhead measured above is unacceptable |
| `lm-format-enforcer` | 0.11.3 | schema enforcement that plugs into `transformers` and `vLLM` generation loops |

## Lab: an extractor that cannot emit invalid output {#sec-decoding-lab}

Build the pipeline, then measure what the guarantee did and did not cover.

### Step 1 — write the schema before the prompt

Fields, types, enums wherever the values are enumerable, and an explicit
nullable for *not present in the source*. The schema is the specification;
the prompt is how you ask for it.

### Step 2 — measure the unenforced baseline

Ask for the schema in the prompt, no enforcement, on 150 items. Record parse
rate, schema-validity, and accuracy. On a strong model expect 98%-ish, which
is the point: **you need this number to know what enforcement is buying.**

### Step 3 — turn the grammar on, and verify it is actually on

Enforce the schema. Then confirm the constraint is live by sending one request
whose schema the model would otherwise violate — @sec-sequence-labeling-llm found a
server silently ignoring `format` on one endpoint while honouring it on
another, and the failure is invisible without this check.

### Step 4 — measure the latency cost, per schema

Time both modes. The overhead here ranged from 1.01× to 17.5× and was not
monotone in schema complexity, so your schema's cost is an empirical question.
If it is large, find out which part of the schema is expensive by removing
fields one at a time.

### Step 5 — count how often valid output is wrong

This is the step the guarantee tempts you to skip. Take the schema-valid
outputs and check the *values* against your labels. Report validity and
accuracy as two separate numbers, because a pipeline can be 100% on the first
and poor on the second, and only one of those is visible in your logs.

### Step 6 — add abstention

Constrain the answer field to a single token, read its logprob, and plot
accuracy against coverage. Pick a threshold on a held-out slice — not on the
data you report — and state the coverage you are shipping at.

### What to hand in

A table with validity, accuracy and latency for enforced and unenforced; the
verification from step 3; the accuracy-versus-coverage curve; and one
paragraph on which failures your guarantee does not cover.

## Exercises {#sec-decoding-exercises}

1. Show algebraically that temperature scaling never changes the argmax
   token. What does this imply about greedy decoding?
2. In the explorer, set $\tau = 1$ and top-k $= 12$. Find the smallest top-p
   that still keeps at least four tokens, and explain the cumulative-mass
   logic behind your answer.
3. Set temperature to 0 and run the same prompt 20 times against a hosted
   API. Are the outputs identical? Explain what you find.
4. Take an extraction task with a 40% JSON failure rate. Add constrained
   decoding and report the new failure rate — and the new error modes.

## Where to go deeper {#sec-decoding-deeper}

Before reading: take one prompt, generate at temperature 0 ten times, and
confirm you get the same string. Whether you do decides how every other number
in your evaluation should be reported.

| resource | what it is |
|:--|:--|
| [`outlines`](https://github.com/dottxt-ai/outlines) | constrained generation as a library; the source is the clearest explanation of the automaton in @sec-decoding-constrained |
| [How to generate text](https://huggingface.co/blog/how-to-generate) — Hugging Face | the decoding strategies with runnable code and honest examples of each one failing |
| [Controllable Text Generation](https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2021-01-02-controllable-text-generation/) — Lilian Weng | a survey-depth post covering the space this chapter samples from |
| [`vllm`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm) | production serving, with structured-output support; read its sampling parameters to see what is actually exposed |
| [Stanford CS336](https://stanford-cs336.github.io/spring2025/) | includes inference and decoding from the implementation side |
| [Let's build GPT: from scratch](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kCc8FmEb1nY) — Andrej Karpathy | the `generate` function written early on, for the bigram baseline, is the simplest possible sampling loop (softmax, then draw a token), in code you can pause and edit; nanoGPT's version adds temperature and top-k |

## What to remember {#sec-decoding-summary}

- **Temperature never changes the ranking.** It rescales logits before the
  softmax, so it controls variance, and lowering it can raise accuracy only up
  to greedy's. If greedy gets an item wrong, a lower temperature makes it
  wrong more reliably.

- **Pick the policy from how many good answers the task has.** One answer:
  greedy or a narrow beam. Many: sample. @sec-machine-translation measured the
  cost of getting it backwards at more than half the BLEU (30.17 → 14.34).

- **Repetition loops are high-probability, not accidental**, which is why
  greedy walks into them. The penalties that fix them are blunt, and they are
  the wrong tool for structured output, where repeated keys and braces are
  correct.

- **On a strong model a grammar buys the last one or two percent.**
  `qwen3.5:9b` was 98–99.3% schema-valid when merely asked, at every schema
  difficulty tested. Enforcement took it to 100% and left accuracy alone.

- **On a weak model it is the difference between working and not.**
  `llama3.2:3b` fell to **79.3%** valid on a nested schema; with the grammar
  it was 100% valid and accuracy rose **70.7% → 88.0%**, because a formatting
  failure had been counted as a reasoning failure.

- **The grammar's cost is latency and it is unpredictable** — 1.01× to **17.5×**
  here, and not monotone in schema complexity. It was worst where the schema
  demanded what the model did not want to produce. Measure it on your schema.

- **A schema guarantees shape, never truth.** `{"answer": 1}` for the capital
  of France is valid, typed and meaningless. Constrained decoding converts
  parse failures into semantic failures, which is a good trade and not a fix.

- **Constrain tool arguments without arguing about it.** 98% is fine for
  extraction and unacceptable when something executes: at a thousand calls a
  day that is twenty wrong actions or stack traces.

- **Logprobs discriminate well and calibrate badly.** AUC **0.9492** against
  the label and **0.8268** for predicting its own correctness, at **7.04%**
  ECE — with the 0.90–0.95 bin right only 68.0% of the time and the bin nearest
  0.5 right on **5 of 15** items, with substantial uncertainty. Rank with them;
  do not quote them as probabilities.

- **Abstention is the cheapest accuracy you will buy.** Dropping the
  least-confident 20% took accuracy from **86.75% to 92.50%** with no model
  change. Choose the threshold on held-out data and report coverage with it.

- **A usable confidence signal is designed in, not discovered.** It worked
  here because the answer was one token from a two-token alphabet. Averaging
  logprobs over free text measures how ordinary the phrasing was.
